blocks.text: Among all possible motions of the material bodies, the circular motion is one that appears to be working in the most of the natural world. Satellites moving in circular orbits around the Earth, orbital and spin motion of the Earth itself, a car turning around a curved road, and a stone whirled around by a string are the familiar examples. When objects move in circular paths, their direction is continuously changing. Since velocity is a vector quantity, this change of direction means that their velocities are not constant.
In this chapter, we will study, circular motion, rotational motion, moment of inertia, angular momentum and the related topics.

Consider an angle drawn at the centre ‘O’ of a circle by an arc ‘AB’ as shown in Fig. 3.1. If the length of the arc ‘AB’ is equal to the radius ‘r’ of the circle, then the angle is called one radian. It is the SI unit of angular measurement and its symbol is “rad”.

blocks.alt: A circle with centre O. Two radii OA and OB, each labelled r, enclose a shaded sector; the arc AB has the same length as the radius, and the angle at O is marked 1 rad. A curved arrow outside the circle runs from A to B.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.1: One radian, the angle at the centre O made by an arc AB equal to the radius r (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.1).
